mishna.en: From when do they recite the Shema in the evening? From the time the priests enter to eat their priestly portion, until the end of the first watch: the opinion of Rabbi Eliezer. The Sages say: Until midnight. Rabban Gamliel says: Until the first light of dawn rises. It happened that his sons came home from a banquet. They said to him, ‘We have not recited the Shema.’ He told them, ‘If the first light of dawn has not risen, you are obligated to recite it.’ Not only in this case: in every case in which the Sages said ‘until midnight,’ the time for performing the commandment extends until the first light of dawn rises. Burning the sacrificial fats and limbs may be performed until the first light of dawn rises. All offerings that are eaten for one day may be eaten until the first light of dawn rises. If so, why did the Sages say ‘until midnight’? To distance a person from transgression.

notes.he: חצות היא הרחקה; בפירוש הרע״ב הקטר חלבים ואברים אינו מוגבל לחצות.
notes.en: Midnight is a safeguard; Bartenura does not apply a midnight limit to burning the fats and limbs.

bartenura.en: ‘From when do they recite? From the time the priests enter to eat their priestly portion.’ Priests who became impure and immersed cannot eat the priestly portion until their sunset has passed, meaning the appearance of the stars. Instead of teaching ‘from the appearance of the stars,’ the Mishna incidentally teaches us that if the priests became impure with an impurity whose purification depends on an offering, such as a man with an abnormal discharge or a person afflicted with tzaraas, their atonement offering does not prevent them from eating the priestly portion. For it is written, ‘The sun shall set and he shall be clean, and afterward he may eat of the sacred things’ (Leviticus 22): his sunset prevents him from eating the priestly portion, but his atonement offering does not prevent him from eating it, etc. ‘Until the end of the first watch.’ The first third of the night, for the night is divided into three watches. After that it is no longer called the time of reciting the Shema associated with lying down, and ‘when you lie down’ does not apply to it. Before the appearance of the stars it is also still daytime, not a time of lying down. Those who recite the evening Shema early, while it is still day, rely on Rabbi Yehudah’s statement below, in the chapter ‘The Morning Prayer,’ that the afternoon prayer may be said until the midpoint of the afternoon period, which is one and a quarter hours before night. We hold that one who follows Rabbi Yehudah has acted validly. As soon as the time for the afternoon prayer ends, the time for the evening Shema begins. ‘Until the first light of dawn rises.’ The entire night is called a time of lying down. The law follows Rabban Gamliel, for the Sages also agree with him; they said ‘until midnight’ only to distance a person from transgression. Nevertheless, as an initial rule, once the time for the evening Shema in our Mishna arrives—that is, from the appearance of the stars—one may not eat a meal, and certainly may not sleep, until one recites the Shema and prays. ‘It happened that his sons came home from a banquet.’ Rabban Gamliel’s sons had heard the Sages say ‘until midnight.’ This is what they asked him: When the Sages disagree with you, do they mean precisely until midnight and no later, in which case, when an individual disputes the majority, the law follows the majority? Or perhaps the Sages agree with you, and say ‘until midnight’ to distance a person from transgression? He told them: The Sages agree with me; they say ‘until midnight’ to distance a person from transgression, and you are obligated to recite it. ‘Not only in this case.’ This entire statement is Rabban Gamliel speaking to his sons. ‘Burning the fats.’ Of the offerings. ‘And limbs.’ Of the afternoon daily burnt offering whose blood was dashed during the day: the commandment is to bring its pieces up throughout the night, as it is written, ‘It is the burnt offering upon its hearth on the altar all night until morning’ (Leviticus 6). ‘All offerings that are eaten for one day.’ Such as the thanksgiving offering, sin offering, guilt offering and the like, which are eaten for a day and a night. Their eating time extends until dawn rises; that is the point that makes them leftover sacrificial meat. ‘If so, why did the Sages say until midnight?’ Concerning the Shema and eating sacred offerings. But for burning the fats and limbs, the Sages did not say ‘until midnight’ at all. It is mentioned here only to teach that anything whose commandment is at night is valid throughout the night. ‘To distance a person from transgression.’ So that he does not come to eat them after dawn rises and become liable to excision; likewise for the Shema, so that he does not say, ‘I still have time,’ and let its appointed time pass.

notes.he: חצות היא הרחקה; בפירוש הרע״ב הקטר חלבים ואברים אינו מוגבל לחצות.
notes.en: Midnight is a safeguard; Bartenura does not apply a midnight limit to burning the fats and limbs.

explanation.he:
הכהנים שטבלו מתחילים לאכול תרומה בצאת הכוכבים; הרע״ב מדגיש שקרבן שעדיין נדרש לטהרתם אינו מעכב אכילה זו. זהו זמן תחילת שמע בערב במשנה. רבי אליעזר מסיים בשליש הלילה הראשון, וחכמים קובעים חצות. רבן גמליאל מחייב את בניו, שחזרו מן המשתה בלי לקרוא, כל עוד לא עלה השחר: כל הלילה הוא זמן שכיבה, וחצות היא סייג מפני דחייה שתביא להחמצה.

הרע״ב מוסיף שמשיגיע זמן הקריאה אסור לסעוד, וכל שכן לישון, לפני שמע ותפילה; תוקף המצווה עד השחר אינו המלצה לאחר. ההסבר שהוא מביא לקריאה מבעוד יום נסמך על שיטת רבי יהודה, ולא משנה את תחילת הזמן במשנה. אברי תמיד בין הערביים, שדמו נזרק ביום, קרבים בלילה; קדשים הנאכלים ליום ולילה נעשים נותר בשחר. סייג חצות נוהג כאן בשמע ובאכילת קדשים, אך לא בהקטר חלבים ואברים.
explanation.en:
The starting point is the appearance of the stars, when priests who immersed may eat the priestly portion. Bartenura explains that an outstanding purification offering does not delay this permission. Rabbi Eliezer ends the reading period after the first third of the night; the Sages say midnight. Rabban Gamliel tells his sons, returning from a banquet without having recited, that they must still recite before dawn: the entire night is a time of lying down, and midnight safeguards against postponing until the opportunity is lost.

This is not advice to delay. Bartenura prohibits eating a meal, and certainly sleeping, once the reading time arrives, before Shema and prayer. His separate explanation of early reading follows Rabbi Yehudah’s timetable, not an earlier starting point in this Mishna. The afternoon daily offering’s limbs, its blood having been dashed by day, may be offered at night; offerings eaten for a day and a night become leftover sacrificial meat at dawn. The midnight safeguard applies here to Shema and eating sacred offerings, not to burning the fats and limbs.

mishna.en: From when do they recite the Shema in the morning? From when one can distinguish between blue and white. Rabbi Eliezer says: Between blue and leek-green. One finishes it by sunrise. Rabbi Yehoshua says: Until three hours into the day, for it is the way of princes to rise at three hours. One who recites from then onward has not lost out: he is like a person reading the Torah.

notes.he: השעות בפירוש הרע״ב הן חלקי היום; שתי הבנות למבחן הצבע נשארות נבדלות.
notes.en: Bartenura measures these hours as portions of daylight and gives two distinct explanations of the color test.

bartenura.en: ‘Between blue and white.’ Between the blue threads and the white threads of the fringes. Another explanation: a fleece dyed blue with places where the dye did not take properly, leaving them white. ‘Between blue and leek-green.’ The blue color is close to the color of leeks, called porosh in the foreign language. ‘Until three hours.’ Into the day: until the end of the third hour, which is a quarter of the day when days and nights are equal. The time for the Shema always extends until a quarter of the day, whether the days are long or short. Likewise, what we learn below (4:1), that the morning prayer may be said until four hours into the day, means until a third of the day. It specifies four hours because a third of the day is four hours when days and nights are equal. Wherever the Mishna mentions so many hours into the day, you must calculate and judge in this way. This is what I understood from the Rambam’s explanations, and I find it acceptable. Rabbi Yehoshua’s reason for saying until three hours into the day is that princes do not rise from their beds until the end of the third hour. When the Merciful One said ‘when you rise,’ He meant until the time at which all people rise from their beds. The law follows Rabbi Yehoshua. Nevertheless, as an initial rule one should arrange to recite the Shema with sunrise, as the devoted early worshippers used to do. ‘Has not lost out.’ He has not lost the right to bless before and after it. Rather, even though its appointed time has passed, he recites it and blesses before and after it. ‘Like a person reading the Torah.’ Although he has not fulfilled the obligation of reciting the Shema at its appointed time, he receives reward like one reading the Torah.

notes.he: השעות בפירוש הרע״ב הן חלקי היום; שתי הבנות למבחן הצבע נשארות נבדלות.
notes.en: Bartenura measures these hours as portions of daylight and gives two distinct explanations of the color test.

explanation.he:
המשנה קושרת את תחילת שמע בבוקר להבחנת צבעים. הרע״ב מביא שני פירושים לתכלת ולבן: חוטי הציצית השונים, או מקומות צבועים ולבנים באותה גיזה. רבי אליעזר מצריך הבחנה בין תכלת לכרתי, שגווניהם קרובים. מול הסיום בהנץ החמה, רבי יהושע מאפשר עד סוף שלוש שעות מפני שגם אז בני מלכים קמים, ועדיין זה זמן קימה.

הרע״ב פוסק כרבי יהושע, אך לכתחילה מכוונים להנץ כוותיקים. שלוש השעות הן רבע היום הארוך או הקצר, לא שלוש שעות שעון קבועות. ההשוואה לארבע שעות של תפילת שחרית מדגימה שליש יום, ואינה מאריכה את זמן שמע. הקורא אחר הזמן מקבל שכר כקורא בתורה אך אינו מקיים שמע בעונתה; הרע״ב מפרש שגם הברכות שלפניה ושלאחריה לא אבדו. זהו ביאור דבריו, לא פסיקה לכל מצב של איחור.
explanation.en:
Daylight must permit a color distinction. Bartenura explains blue and white either as different fringe threads or as dyed and undyed patches in one fleece. Rabbi Eliezer requires distinguishing the closer colors blue and leek-green. Against the sunrise finishing point, Rabbi Yehoshua permits until the end of three hours because princes still rise then: this remains part of human rising-time.

Bartenura follows Rabbi Yehoshua, while identifying reading with sunrise as the initial ideal. Three hours means a quarter of the daylight period, whether long or short—not three fixed clock hours. His comparison with morning prayer until four hours illustrates a third of the day, not an extension of Shema’s time. Reading afterward earns the reward of Torah reading but does not fulfill Shema at its appointed time. He explains that the preceding and following blessings are not lost either. This explains his commentary rather than deciding every practical late-reading case.

mishna.en: Bais Shammai say: In the evening everyone should recline and recite, and in the morning they should stand, as it says, ‘When you lie down and when you rise’ (Deuteronomy 6). Bais Hillel say: Everyone recites in his usual manner, as it says, ‘When you walk on the road’ (ibid.). If so, why does it say ‘when you lie down and when you rise’? At the time people lie down and at the time people rise. Rabbi Tarfon said: I was traveling on the road and reclined to recite, following the opinion of Bais Shammai, and put myself in danger from robbers. They told him: You would have deserved to incur the consequences yourself, because you transgressed the words of Bais Hillel.

bartenura.en: ‘Should recline.’ On their sides, for it is written ‘when you lie down’: in a lying position. ‘Should stand.’ For it is written ‘when you rise’: in a standing position. ‘In his usual manner.’ Whether standing, sitting, lying down or walking. ‘You would have deserved.’ You would have deserved to be killed; had you died, you would have been responsible for your own life.

explanation.he:
בית שמאי מפרשים ובשכבך ובקומך כתנוחות: בערב להטות על הצד ובבוקר לעמוד. בית הלל לומדים מכאן זמני שכיבה וקימה, ולא חובה לשנות תנוחה; ובלכתך בדרך מלמד על קריאה במהלך החיים הרגיל. הרע״ב מפרט עמידה, ישיבה, שכיבה והליכה.

רבי טרפון הטה בדרך כבית שמאי ונחשף לסכנת לסטים. החכמים אינם משבחים את החומרה, אלא מוכיחים אותו על שעבר על דברי בית הלל. הרע״ב מפרש שאילו נהרג, היה אחראי לנפשו. אין אפוא להציג את ההסתכנות בשם השיטה האחרת כהידור רצוי. רשימת התנוחות מבארת את המחלוקת הזאת, ולא את כל דיני הכוונה והקריאה.
explanation.en:
Bais Shammai read “when you lie down and when you rise” as prescribing posture: reclining on one’s side in the evening and standing in the morning. Bais Hillel read these as the usual times of lying down and rising, not a demand to change posture. “When you walk on the road” allows reading during ordinary activity. Bartenura lists standing, sitting, lying down and walking.

Rabbi Tarfon reclined while traveling to follow Bais Shammai and exposed himself to robbers. The Sages rebuke rather than praise this stringency, because he went against Bais Hillel. Bartenura explains that, had he been killed, he would have borne responsibility for his own life. The episode does not recommend dangerous imitation of the other school’s practice. The posture list explains this dispute, not every requirement of attention and recitation.

mishna.en: In the morning one says two blessings before it and one after it; in the evening, two before it and two after it. One is long and one short. Where they said to make a blessing long, one may not make it short; where they said to make it short, one may not make it long. Where they said to conclude with a blessing, one may not omit that conclusion; where they said not to conclude with a blessing, one may not add that conclusion.

notes.he: ארוכה וקצרה מוסבות בפירוש הרע״ב על צורת הברכות שלפניה, ולא על רשות לשנות את נוסחן.
notes.en: Bartenura relates long and short to the form of the preceding blessings, not permission to rewrite their wording.

bartenura.en: ‘Two before it.’ ‘Who forms light’ and the blessing of love. ‘One after it.’ ‘True and established.’ ‘In the evening.’ One blesses. ‘Two before it.’ ‘Who brings on evenings’ and ‘Everlasting love.’ ‘Two after it.’ ‘True and faithful’ and ‘Make us lie down.’ ‘One long and one short.’ This refers to the two before it. ‘Who forms light’ is long, opening with ‘Blessed’ and concluding with ‘Blessed,’ as does ‘Who brings on evenings.’ The blessing of love is short: it concludes with ‘Blessed’ but does not open with ‘Blessed.’ ‘To conclude.’ With ‘Blessed.’ ‘Not to conclude.’ Such as the blessing over fruit and the blessing over commandments.

notes.he: ארוכה וקצרה מוסבות בפירוש הרע״ב על צורת הברכות שלפניה, ולא על רשות לשנות את נוסחן.
notes.en: Bartenura relates long and short to the form of the preceding blessings, not permission to rewrite their wording.

explanation.he:
בבוקר אומרים שתי ברכות לפני שמע ואחת אחריה, ובערב שתיים לפניה ושתיים אחריה. הרע״ב מזהה בבוקר יוצר אור ואהבה, ואחר הקריאה אמת ויציב; בערב מעריב ערבים ואהבת עולם, ואחריה אמת ואמונה והשכיבנו.

ארוכה וקצרה מוסבות אצלו על שתי הברכות שלפניה: יוצר אור ומעריב ערבים פותחות וחותמות בברוך; אהבה חותמת אך אינה פותחת בברוך. זו הבחנה בצורה, לא במשך הקריאה או רשות לקצר את הנוסח. יש לשמור על התקנה: לא להחליף ארוכה וקצרה, לא להשמיט חתימה נדרשת ולא להוסיף חתימה שלא נקבעה. ברכות הפירות והמצוות מדגימות ברכות שאין להן חתימה כזאת.
explanation.en:
Morning has two blessings before Shema and one after; evening has two before and two after. Bartenura identifies the morning blessings as those about forming light and love, followed by “True and established.” Evening has the blessings about bringing on evenings and everlasting love, followed by “True and faithful” and “Make us lie down.”

He relates long and short to the two preceding blessings: the blessings about forming light and bringing on evenings open and conclude with “Blessed”; the blessing of love concludes that way but does not open that way. This concerns structure, not duration or permission to abridge. Preserve the prescribed forms: do not exchange long and short, omit a required conclusion, or add an unprescribed conclusion. Blessings over fruit and commandments exemplify blessings without that separate conclusion.

mishna.en: The departure from Egypt is mentioned at night. Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah said: I am like a man of seventy, yet I did not prevail in having the departure from Egypt said at night until Ben Zoma expounded it, as it says, ‘So that you remember the day you left the land of Egypt all the days of your life’ (Deuteronomy 16). ‘The days of your life’ means the days; ‘all the days of your life’ includes the nights. The Sages say: ‘The days of your life’ means this world; ‘all the days of your life’ includes the days of the Messiah.

bartenura.en: ‘The departure from Egypt is mentioned at night.’ The passage about fringes is said in the evening Shema. Although night is not the time for fringes—for ‘you shall see it’ excludes a nighttime garment—it is said at night because it contains the departure from Egypt. ‘Like a man of seventy.’ I appeared old: not actually old, but his hair turned white on the day they appointed him leader so that he would look old and fit for leadership. That very day Ben Zoma expounded this verse. ‘I did not prevail.’ I did not defeat the Sages in argument. A similar expression occurs in the Talmud, in the chapter ‘Daughters of Samaritans’ (Niddah 38b): ‘In this Rabbi Elazar prevailed over the Rabbis,’ meaning that he defeated them in argument.

explanation.he:
הרע״ב מסביר שאומרים פרשת ציצית בשמע של ערבית מפני יציאת מצרים שבה, אף שהלילה אינו זמן ציצית לפי הדרשה שהוא מביא. תפקיד הפרשה בקריאה ודין לבישת ציצית בלילה הם עניינים נבדלים.

כבן שבעים אינו גיל ממש: שער רבי אלעזר בן עזריה הלבין ביום מינויו לנשיא כדי שייראה ראוי לתפקיד; באותו יום דרש בן זומא. ולא זכיתי פירושו שלא ניצח את החכמים בוויכוח, לא שלא קיים את המצווה. בן זומא דורש ימי חייך לימים, וכל ימי חייך גם ללילות. החכמים דורשים ימי חייך לעולם הזה, וכל גם לימות המשיח. אלו שימושים שונים בריבוי כל; אין למזג את שתי הדרשות.
explanation.en:
Bartenura explains that the fringes passage is recited in the evening Shema because it mentions the departure from Egypt, although night is not the time for fringes under the interpretation he cites. The passage’s role in the reading and the nighttime clothing rule are distinct.

“Like a man of seventy” is not a statement of actual age: Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah’s hair turned white on his appointment as leader so he would appear suited to the office. Ben Zoma expounded the verse that day. “I did not prevail” means not overcoming the Sages in argument, not failing to perform the commandment. Ben Zoma reads “the days of your life” as days and “all” as adding nights. The Sages read the first phrase as this world and “all” as adding the days of the Messiah. These are distinct uses of the expansion, not one combined derivation.
